caveats: City of Los Angeles streets only. Venues in Inglewood, Long Beach, Pasadena, Carson, Anaheim, and other cities have little or no data here.

The venue list is the city's unofficial, subject-to-change LA28 list, not the current LA28 Games Plan.

organizer_technologies.title: National para-sport activity
organizer_technologies.description: Before Paris, the French Paralympic and Sports Committee published what clubs and programs were already doing. That kind of report is the community baseline, not a Games-time app.

organizer_technologies.title: One supporter database
organizer_technologies.description: Paris 2024 kept a single record for people who joined through social media, the website, or a ticket. Surveys then fed sport-specific email and SMS journeys in five languages.

organizer_technologies.title: A public channel
organizer_technologies.description: The International Paralympic Committee used TikTok for match clips, athlete live video, daily highlights, and short explainers of the 22 sports.

organizer_technologies.title: Access tools at the venue
organizer_technologies.description: Spectators could use audio description in the official app, a low-vision helmet, tactile tablets, captions, and sign language. These sit on top of the channels above.

planning_notes.text: Paris used 20 Paralympic competition venues alongside 41 Olympic competition venues
Some venues hosted different sports in the Olympic and Paralympic periods — rapid changes to seating, equipment, layouts, tech, and spectator facilities
Overnight conversions were extremely tight (example: ~17 hours between sports at Bercy Arena)
LA28 has published a Paralympic venue plan centered on accessibility and athlete experience
Confirm sports and sites on the official LA28 venues and Paralympic pages
Step-free journeys from transit stations to seats, including sidewalks, ramps, shuttles, and drop-offs
Accessible seating, restrooms, entrances, signage, and evacuation procedures at venues
Digital platforms (tickets, apps, travel info) need WCAG-style accessibility
Communication supports: ASL, captions, audio description, assistive listening
Test venues and transportation with disabled users before public opening
Accessibility improvements should remain after 2028 — not only for Games time
Paris mobilized ~12,000 private security agents during the Paralympic Games (vs ~23,000 during the Olympics)
Security plans must stay accessible for people with disabilities
Volunteers and staff need disability-awareness and assistance training
California is developing Olympic and Paralympic public-safety coordination agreements
Multi-city venues mean security coordination across jurisdictions
Which venue has the most corners without a ramp, and which has the highest share? Would the same fix work for both?
Pick one city LA28 site above and map the walk from the nearest Metro station. Where would a wheelchair user have to detour?
Walk or map Expo Park/USC station to the Coliseum and Pico station to LA Live. How many crossings are there, and does every corner have a ramp?
Inglewood, Long Beach, and Pasadena venues have little data here. Which agency keeps their curb-ramp records, and is it public?
A ramp can exist and still be too steep, cracked, or blocked. What would you check on site before calling a route step-free?

sections.heading: Street access near venues
sections.text: Street access near venues Added at the request of a student team researching accessible passageways for disabled spectators. The City of Los Angeles records whether each street corner within about a mile of its LA28 venue list has a curb ramp. A missing ramp means a wheelchair user has to detour or roll into the street. sections.heading: Organizer technology map
sections.text: Organizer technology map A teaching map of public systems Paris organizers used for community engagement and accessible spectating. The boxes are separate tools. They connect because each one answers a different question: who is already involved, who to message, where the Paralympics are published, and how a disabled spectator follows the action. 01 Record the community National para-sport activity Before Paris, the French Paralympic and Sports Committee published what clubs and programs were already doing. That kind of report is the community baseline, not a Games-time app. Comité Paralympique et Sportif Français 02 Know who to reach One supporter database Paris 2024 kept a single record for people who joined through social media, the website, or a ticket. Surveys then fed sport-specific email and SMS journeys in five languages. Salesforce, Paris 2024 story 03 Publish the Paralympics A public channel The International Paralympic Committee used TikTok for match clips, athlete live video, daily highlights, and short explainers of the 22 sports. International Paralympic Committee 04 Follow the event live Access tools at the venue Spectators could use audio description in the official app, a low-vision helmet, tactile tablets, captions, and sign language. These sit on top of the channels above. sportanddev A second student reference, an Olympic World Library file, did not open outside a browser cookie check, so this map does not describe its contents.
